chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Anita notices that her rotis puff up on a hot tawa but not on a warm one. What is the best first step to find out why?
b: Ask her friend to guess the answer
c: Ask a clear, testable question and observe carefully
d: Stop because science cannot explain cooking
why: Every investigation begins with curiosity turned into a clear question that can be tested.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Why should a student note down observations while doing an experiment?
b: So the teacher need not check it
d: So the results can be checked and compared later
why: Written records let you check, compare and repeat the work; memory can fail.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: In a fair test, how many conditions should you change at one time?
why: Changing one condition at a time shows which condition caused the result.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Which of these is a question that science can test?
a: Which colour is the most beautiful?
b: Does a plant grow taller in sunlight than in shade?
d: Which song is nicest to hear?
why: Science can answer questions that can be tested by observation or measurement; opinions of beauty cannot be measured.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: A hypothesis in an investigation is best described as
b: A random guess nobody can check
c: A possible answer that can be tested
why: A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation; the experiment then supports or rejects it.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Sunita compares how fast sugar dissolves in 100 mL of cold water and 100 mL of hot water, using one spoon of the same sugar. What is the variable she changes?
why: Only the water temperature differs; everything else is kept the same.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Which of the following is an observation and not an opinion?
a: The paper turned brown after 10 minutes in the sun
d: The sun is unfair to paper
why: An observation is what you can see, measure or record, without adding personal judgement.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Which statement best describes how science grows?
a: Once written in a book, ideas never change
b: New evidence can improve or change earlier explanations
c: Only one scientist decides what is true
why: Science is self-correcting: new observations can refine or replace old ideas.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Rahul tests which paper plane flies farthest. He uses A4 paper for plane P and a thicker chart paper for plane Q, and throws P gently and Q hard. Which statement is correct?
a: The test is fair because two planes are used
b: The test is fair because he threw both
c: The test is unfair only because the planes are of the same shape
d: The test is unfair because paper type and throwing force both differ
why: Two conditions changed together, so a difference in distance cannot be linked to one cause.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Arrange these steps of an investigation in the correct order: (1) draw a conclusion, (2) ask a question, (3) do the experiment and record results, (4) make a hypothesis.
why: We ask a question, propose a hypothesis, test and record, and then conclude.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Priya wants to know if the amount of oil affects how much a puri puffs. Which of these should she keep the same?
b: Dough, thickness, flame and frying time
why: All factors except the one being tested must be controlled.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Four students recorded the temperature of cooling tea every 2 minutes. Which record is best?
a: A single reading at the end
c: A table showing time and temperature with units
d: A drawing of the cup only
why: Repeated, measured values with units make a clear and checkable record.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: A student repeats an experiment three times and gets 20 s, 21 s and 20 s. What does this suggest?
d: The result is reliable because it is nearly the same each time
why: Repeating and getting close values increases trust in the result.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: After testing, Ravi's result does not match his hypothesis. What is the best thing for him to do?
a: Accept the result and revise the hypothesis
b: Change the result to match his hypothesis
why: A good scientist follows the evidence even when it disagrees with the hypothesis.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Meera tests how the height of a ramp changes the distance a toy car rolls. Which two quantities should she measure?
a: Colour of car and ramp height
c: Mass of ramp and time of day
d: Distance rolled and the colour of floor
why: She changes ramp height and measures the distance the car rolls in response.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Which question is the most suitable for a scientific investigation at school?
b: Who invented the pendulum first in history books?
c: How does the length of a pendulum affect the time of 10 swings?
d: Will pendulums be popular next year?
why: It can be tested by measuring with a stopwatch while changing only the length.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Ravi tests whether salt dissolves faster in hot water. He puts 1 spoon of fine salt in 100 mL hot water and 1 spoon of coarse salt in 100 mL cold water. Why can he not conclude anything about temperature?
a: Both temperature and grain size changed
b: The volume of water was different
c: Salt does not dissolve in cold water
why: With two variables changed, a faster result could be due to either temperature or grain size.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: A student claims that plants kept in a cupboard grow slower than those in the window, so sunlight makes them grow faster. The cupboard is also cooler. What is the weakness in her claim?
a: Plants never grow in a cupboard
b: Temperature also differs, so sunlight alone is not shown to be the cause
why: A second difference (temperature) could also explain the result, so she cannot be sure about sunlight.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Over 5 days, a bean seedling grows 2 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm, 8 cm and 40 cm. What is the most sensible action?
b: Write that the seedling grew by magic
c: Recheck the 40 cm reading, since it breaks the pattern
d: Average only the last two readings
why: A reading far from the pattern is possibly a recording or measuring error and should be rechecked.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Two groups did the same experiment on boiling time of water at the same flame. Group A got 6 min, Group B got 9 min. Which is the most likely reason?
a: Water boils differently for each group
b: Group B used a bad clock only
d: The volume of water or the flame size was not the same
why: Unless amount of water and heat are controlled, results differ even for the same procedure.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: To find out whether the number of turns of a coil changes the number of paper clips an electromagnet lifts, Gita uses 20 turns with a thin wire and a 1.5 V cell, and 40 turns with a thick wire and a 3 V cell. What should she do?
a: Use the same wire and the same cell, changing only the turns
d: Keep the coils different so results are more interesting
why: Only the number of turns should change; wire and cell must stay the same.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: A hypothesis says: "Heavier stones fall faster." An experiment shows a 100 g stone and a 500 g stone reaching the ground together when dropped from the same height. Which conclusion is best?
b: The hypothesis is not supported by this evidence
c: The experiment is invalid because the stones are heavy
why: Experiments can show a hypothesis is not supported; here the weights did not change the fall time.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Why is a statement like "All swans are white" never fully proven in science, even after seeing thousands of white swans?
c: One observation of a non-white swan can disprove it
d: Thousands of observations are too few to count
why: A single counter-example can disprove a general claim, while many examples cannot prove it for certain.

chapter: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
question: Kavya wants to find if the colour of a cloth affects how hot it gets in sunlight. She sets a black cloth in the open and a white cloth in shade, both of the same size, and finds the black one hotter. Which change makes the test fair and still answers her question?
c: Put the black cloth in a bigger room
d: Place both cloths in the same sunny spot for the same time
why: Colour must be the only difference; location and exposure time must be identical.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which instrument do we need to see most microorganisms?
why: Microorganisms are too small for the naked eye, so a microscope is used.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which microorganism makes dough rise when added to flour for bhature?
why: Yeast ferments sugar and releases carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which of these is a fungus?
why: Moulds and yeast are fungi; Lactobacillus and Rhizobium are bacteria; Amoeba is a protozoan.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Rhizobium bacteria live in the root nodules of which crop?
why: Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the roots of legumes such as chana, moong and peas.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which gas turns lime water milky?
why: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to form a white, milky solid.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which place helps mould grow fastest on bread?
why: Microbes grow best with warmth and moisture.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which of these is both a plant-cell part and absent in an animal cell?
why: Plant cells have a cell wall outside the membrane; animal cells do not.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Curd forms from milk because of
why: Lactobacillus turns milk sugar into lactic acid, which makes milk set into curd.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Why do we keep cooked dal in a refrigerator?
a: Low temperature slows down growth of microbes
why: Low temperature slows microbial growth and delays spoilage.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: A balloon is tied over a bottle with yeast, sugar and warm water. After a day the balloon is inflated. The gas inside is mainly
why: Yeast ferments sugar and gives off carbon dioxide.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: A farmer grows moong and does not add nitrogen fertiliser, but a neighbour growing maize does. Why?
a: Moong does not need any nutrients
b: Maize bacteria fix nitrogen in leaves
c: Moong has Rhizobium in its root nodules that fixes nitrogen
d: Moong takes nitrogen only from rain
why: Legume roots host nitrogen-fixing bacteria; maize cannot use air nitrogen.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Two pits are filled with vegetable peels. Pit A is kept moist and covered with soil; Pit B is kept dry. After 3 weeks, A has decomposed far more. What does this show?
d: Decomposers need moisture to work well
why: Decomposer microbes need moisture; the damp pit decomposes faster.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which pair is correctly matched?
why: Yeast is a fungus; Amoeba is a protozoan; Lactobacillus and Rhizobium are bacteria.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Bread slice X is kept in a closed box in the kitchen; slice Y is kept in a fridge. After 3 days only X has mould. Which factor best explains it?
a: Closed box lets in more light
why: Mould spores grow quickly at room temperature but slowly in the cold.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Curd kept outside for 24 hours becomes more sour. A likely reason is
c: Lactobacillus kept multiplying and made more lactic acid
why: More bacteria produce more lactic acid, so the taste turns more sour.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: A virus differs from bacteria in that it
d: Multiplies only inside a living host cell
why: Viruses cannot reproduce on their own; they need a host cell.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: A compost heap is turned and sprinkled with water weekly, yet decomposes slowly in winter. The most likely reason is
why: Microbial activity falls in the cold, even when air and moisture are available.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Lime water is placed in a test tube connected to a flask of sugar and yeast. After 4 hours it turns milky. A student repeats the setup without yeast. What will she find and why?
a: It turns milkier because sugar gives carbon dioxide
b: It becomes blue as sugar rises
c: It stays clear because no carbon dioxide is made without yeast
d: It turns milky because air alone makes CO2
why: Without yeast there is no fermentation, so no carbon dioxide reaches the lime water.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: To test whether moisture is needed for mould growth, which set-up is best?
a: A damp slice in a fridge and a dry slice in sunlight
b: Two damp slices at different temperatures
d: Two identical slices, one damp and one dry, kept at the same temperature
why: Only moisture should differ; temperature and bread type stay equal.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: If all decomposers on Earth died, what would happen first?
a: Dead matter would pile up and nutrients would not return to soil
why: Decomposers recycle nutrients; without them waste builds up and soil nutrients run out.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Which statement about microorganisms is correct?
b: Some are useful and some cause disease
d: All can be seen without a microscope
why: Microbes include helpful ones (curd, bread, antibiotics) and harmful pathogens.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Yeast is added to two flasks of sugar solution. Flask P is kept at 35 degrees C and flask Q at 5 degrees C. After 3 hours, which observation is most likely?
a: More bubbles in Q because cold makes yeast faster
c: More bubbles in P because yeast is more active when warm
d: No bubbles in P because heat kills yeast at 35 degrees C
why: Yeast ferments faster at a warm, moderate temperature; at 5 degrees C it is slow.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: Fresh milk boiled and sealed in a clean airtight bottle stays unspoilt for many days, while open milk spoils in a day. Which reasoning is best?
d: Boiling kills most microbes and sealing keeps new ones out
why: Heat kills microbes and the closed bottle prevents new ones from entering.

chapter: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
question: A field of arhar (a legume) was ploughed in after harvest, then wheat was sown with less fertiliser than usual. Why is this practice useful?
a: Legume roots left nitrogen compounds in the soil for the next crop
b: Wheat fixes nitrogen from the ploughed roots
d: Ploughing adds Rhizobium to wheat leaves
why: Nitrogen fixed by Rhizobium enriches the soil, reducing fertiliser needed.

question: Which of these diseases spreads from one person to another?
why: Cholera is communicable; the others do not spread person to person.

question: The best way to prevent many stomach infections is to
b: Wash hands with soap before eating
why: Handwashing removes germs before they enter the mouth.

question: Which pair contains only non-communicable diseases?
why: Diabetes and asthma do not spread from person to person.

question: Malaria is spread by
why: Anopheles females carry the malaria parasite.

question: Antibiotics work against
why: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria and do not act on viruses.

question: Vaccines help the body by
b: Training the immune system to fight a germ
d: Making us immune to every disease
why: A vaccine prepares the immune system so it responds faster to the real germ.

question: Why should stagnant water be removed near homes?
why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in standing water.

question: Which one is a lifestyle habit that raises the risk of non-communicable disease?
why: Tobacco increases the risk of lung disease, cancer and heart disease.

question: Which pair of diseases mainly spreads through contaminated water?
why: Cholera and typhoid spread through food or water carrying germs from excreta.

question: Rohit has a viral cold and asks the chemist for antibiotics. A good reply is that
c: Antibiotics do not work against viruses and may cause resistance
d: Antibiotics work faster on viruses than bacteria
why: Antibiotics act on bacteria; unnecessary use helps resistant bacteria develop.

question: A family returns from a trip to a mosquito-prone area and a child develops fever with chills. What is the most sensible step?
c: Hide from people for a year
d: Visit a doctor for tests and treatment
why: Fever after exposure could be malaria; diagnosis and proper treatment matter.

question: A classmate says diabetes spreads by sharing food. Which reply is correct?
a: Diabetes is non-communicable, so it does not spread that way
why: Diabetes is related to the body's sugar control, not germs.

question: Why is it important to finish a full antibiotic course prescribed by a doctor?
b: Stopping early can leave some bacteria that may become resistant
why: Surviving bacteria after incomplete treatment may develop resistance.

question: Which set of habits best reduces dengue spread?
c: Empty coolers weekly, use nets and repellents
why: Dengue mosquitoes breed in clean standing water, so removing it plus personal protection helps.

question: After chicken pox most people do not get it again. This is mainly because
d: The immune system remembers the virus
why: Memory cells respond quickly on a second meeting with the same germ.

question: Which statement is correct?
a: Communicable diseases are caused by germs and can spread
b: All diseases are caused by germs
why: Communicable diseases come from pathogens; non-communicable ones do not pass between people.

question: In a town, dengue cases were 20 in April, 35 in June, 150 in August, 210 in September and 60 in November. Which explanation best fits the pattern?
a: Dengue is caused by cold winds
c: Monsoon rain increases standing water and mosquito breeding
why: Rain collects in containers, so mosquitoes breed and cases rise after the monsoon.

question: A person gets chicken pox once but gets cold many times. Why can colds recur?
d: Many different cold viruses exist and they change
why: Immune memory works against a specific germ; many varieties cause common colds.

question: Which advice does NOT help prevent a non-communicable disease?
a: Take antibiotics regularly to stay healthy
why: Antibiotics act on bacteria and do not prevent lifestyle diseases.

question: A village well gets sewage seepage and many people suffer vomiting and diarrhoea. Which step is best for the community?
b: Chlorinate the water and stop sewage entering the well
why: Disinfecting water and sealing the contamination source breaks the disease cycle.

question: Two children are given the same vaccine. Child P is later exposed to the germ and recovers in 2 days; Child Q, unvaccinated, is ill for 10 days. The best explanation is
a: P has more antibiotics in blood
b: Q has no white blood cells at all
c: The memory cells in P responded faster
why: A vaccinated child has memory cells that respond quickly.

question: Which pair of examples is correctly classed?
why: Measles spreads by a virus; asthma is not infectious.

question: A doctor says resistance is increasing. Which action by patients makes it worse?
a: Taking antibiotics for viral fevers and stopping midway
b: Completing the course for bacterial infection
why: Overuse and incomplete use give resistant bacteria a chance to survive.

question: Which plan best reduces both malaria and dengue in a colony?
b: Stop water collecting in containers, use nets and repellent, spray as advised
why: Controlling breeding sites and bites tackles both mosquito-borne diseases.

question: A current-carrying wire placed near a compass needle will
why: Electric current produces a magnetic field that deflects a compass.

question: Which appliance works mainly on the heating effect of current?
why: An electric iron has a heating element; a bell works on the magnetic effect.

question: A cell converts
why: A cell stores chemicals that react to produce an electric current.

question: Heating wires in toasters are made of nichrome because it
a: Has high resistance and does not oxidise easily when hot
why: Nichrome gets very hot and resists burning in air.

question: An electromagnet is made by passing current through a coil wound on
why: Iron strengthens the magnetic field of the coil and loses it when current stops.

question: Which liquid will make a bulb in a simple cell circuit glow better?
why: Lemon juice has ions that conduct electricity; pure water and oils do not.

question: What happens to an electromagnet when the current is switched off?
why: An electromagnet is a magnet only while current flows.

question: Which will heat up faster for the same current and material?
b: A thick nichrome wire of equal length
why: A thinner wire has higher resistance, so more heat is produced.

question: A coil with 20 turns picks up 6 pins. Which change would most likely make it pick up more?
c: Increase the turns and use the same cell
why: More turns and a stronger current increase the magnetism.

question: In a lemon cell, a copper strip and a zinc strip are pushed into a lemon. The lemon juice acts as
why: The juice carries ions between the metals, completing the circuit inside the cell.

question: Why do electric fuses melt when the current is too large?
a: Large current produces enough heat to melt the thin wire
d: Electricity changes the wire to water
why: The heating effect protects other appliances by breaking the circuit.

question: If the battery connections of a wire near a compass are reversed, the needle deflection will
why: Reversing current reverses the direction of the magnetic field.

question: Which change makes a compass placed near a straight current-carrying wire deflect more?
c: Using a larger current in the wire
why: A stronger current produces a stronger magnetic field; reversing it only reverses the direction of deflection.

question: Four cups hold: tap water with salt, pure water, sugar solution and plain oil. A cell is dipped into each in turn. Which makes a bulb glow?
why: Salt gives ions that conduct; sugar solution, pure water and oil do not conduct well.

question: Which of the following does an electric bell use?
why: An electromagnet pulls the hammer repeatedly to ring the bell.

question: A thick copper wire connects an electric heater to the socket. The heater element glows red but the copper wire stays cool. Why?
b: Copper has very low resistance and the nichrome element has high resistance
c: The same current cannot flow through copper
d: Nichrome is a better conductor than copper
why: The same current flows through both, but heat is produced mainly where the resistance is high.

question: Meena's electromagnet lifted 10 pins when connected to a fresh cell. After an hour, it lifts 2 pins though the wire is still warm. The best explanation is
d: The cell is running down so current is weaker
why: A weaker current gives a weaker magnetic effect while some heating remains.

question: A circuit is made with a cell, an LED and two metal strips dipped in a glass. The LED glows when the glass has lemon juice but not with sugar solution. A student says sugar cannot be an electrolyte because it is sweet. What is the correct reasoning?
a: Sugar dissolves as molecules, not ions, so it does not conduct
d: Juice is a conductor only in dark
why: Conduction in solutions needs charged ions; sugar does not form ions.

question: Two nichrome wires, X and Y, are of the same thickness. X is 20 cm long and Y is 40 cm. Connected one by one to the same cell, which statement is most likely?
a: X has more resistance than Y
b: Y has more resistance and shows less current
c: Both have exactly the same resistance
why: A longer wire has greater resistance, so less current flows.

question: A coil without an iron core deflects a compass by 10 degrees. When an iron nail is placed inside, the deflection
why: Soft iron inside the coil strengthens the magnetic field.

question: A bulb is in series with a thin nichrome wire and a cell, and glows dimly. The nichrome wire is replaced by a copper wire of the same length and thickness. The bulb will now glow
a: More dimly, since copper has higher resistance
b: Equally, since both wires carry current
c: Not at all, since copper is an insulator
d: More brightly, since copper has much lower resistance
why: Less resistance in the circuit lets a larger current flow through the bulb.

question: The heating effect makes a fuse useful. Which fuse wire is suited to a 5 A circuit?
a: A wire that melts at a little above 5 A
b: A wire that melts at 0.1 A
d: A wire that melts at 100 A
why: A fuse should melt only when the current becomes dangerously more than the rated value.

question: A crane uses an electromagnet to lift scrap iron and drop it at a different place. Why is an electromagnet better than a permanent magnet?
b: Its magnetism can be switched off to drop the load
why: Switching the current off releases the iron.

question: Raju makes two fruit cells in series, and the LED glows. When he takes one cell out the LED dims. Which reasoning is best?
b: Series cells use up the LED
c: Voltage from two cells is higher than from one
d: The LED needs light to glow
why: Two cells in series add their voltage, so more current flows.

question: A force can be a
why: A force is described as a push or pull on an object.

question: Friction acts
a: In the same direction as motion
d: Opposite to the direction of motion
why: Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces.

question: Which is a non-contact force?
why: Gravity acts without touching the object.

question: Mass of an object is measured in
why: Mass is measured in kg; weight (a force) is measured in newtons.

question: Which surface produces the most friction?
why: Rougher surfaces have more interlocking and so more friction.

question: A plastic comb rubbed on dry hair attracts small paper bits because
why: Rubbing charges the comb, which attracts light paper pieces.

question: An iron nail sinks in water because its
a: Weight is greater than the upward buoyant force
why: If weight is more than buoyancy, the object sinks.

question: The force with which Earth pulls an object is called
why: Weight is the gravitational pull on an object.

question: Why do we sprinkle sand on a wet slippery road?
why: Sand makes the surface rough and increases grip.

question: An astronaut weighs 600 N on Earth. On the Moon, where gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's, her weight will be about
why: 600 / 6 = 100 N. Mass stays the same; weight changes.

question: Which of these does NOT need contact between objects?
b: A magnet attracting an iron nail
why: A magnetic force can act across a gap.

question: A wooden block of 100 cm cubic volume floats in water but a steel ball of the same weight sinks. Why?
c: Steel ball has smaller volume so less water is displaced
why: Buoyancy depends on displaced water volume; the larger block displaces more.

question: A box needs 50 N to start moving on a floor and 40 N to keep it moving. Which statement is correct?
b: Friction is zero when the box moves
d: Starting friction is greater than moving friction
why: It takes more force to start motion than to continue it.

question: Two balloons rubbed on hair are brought close. They
why: Like charges repel; both balloons carry the same kind of charge.

question: A ball is thrown straight up. At the highest point, the force acting on it is
why: Gravity acts all the time; the throw force ends when the ball leaves the hand.

question: A cricket ball moving along the ground slows and stops. Which force mainly stops it?
why: The ground exerts friction opposing the motion.

question: A 12 kg bag on the Moon (gravity about 1/6 of Earth's, taking Earth's g as 10 N/kg) has weight
why: On the Moon g = 10/6; weight = 12 x 10/6 = 20 N. The mass is still 12 kg.

question: A student pushes a heavy almirah and it does not move even though she pushes with 200 N. What can be said about the friction force?
b: It is also 200 N, balancing her push
c: It is more than 200 N and acts forward
why: For no motion, forces balance: static friction equals the push.

question: Two blocks of equal volume are held fully under water. Block P has mass 200 g and block Q has mass 400 g. Which statement about the buoyant force is correct?
a: It is greater on Q because Q is heavier
b: It is greater on P because P is lighter
c: It is the same on both because they displace equal volumes
why: Buoyant force equals the weight of water displaced, which depends only on the volume under water.

question: A satellite moves around Earth in a circle at constant speed. Which statement is correct?
a: No force acts since its speed is constant
b: The force acts only when it speeds up
c: Force acts only along its direction of motion
d: A force (gravity) acts on it because its direction keeps changing
why: Force is needed to change direction as well as speed; gravity pulls the satellite toward Earth.

question: A spring balance shows 49 N for an object on Earth taking g = 9.8 m/s squared. Its mass is
why: Mass = weight / g = 49 / 9.8 = 5 kg.

question: Why is friction both useful and harmful in a bicycle?
b: Brakes need friction while chain moving parts waste energy as heat
c: Friction only acts in the tyres
d: Friction only acts in the air
why: Friction provides grip in brakes and tyres but wears the chain, so we oil it.

question: A piece of wax floats in water but sinks in kerosene. What can be concluded?
c: Wax is denser than kerosene and less dense than water
why: It floats where the liquid is denser than wax, and sinks where the liquid is less dense.

question: A girl pulls a sled with 30 N to the right and her brother pulls with 45 N to the left. Which is the net force?
why: Opposite forces subtract: 45 - 30 = 15 N toward the larger force.

question: Pressure is defined as
why: Pressure = force / area.

question: A force of 200 N acts on an area of 4 square metres. The pressure is
why: 200 / 4 = 50 N per square metre = 50 Pa.

question: Pressure in a liquid at rest increases with
why: The deeper you go, the greater the weight of liquid above.

question: Air moves from
b: Cold place to cold place only
why: Wind is air flowing from a region of higher pressure to lower pressure.

question: Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt one?
a: Larger edge area gives larger pressure
c: It has less friction in air
d: Smaller edge area gives larger pressure
why: For the same force, a smaller area gives more pressure.

question: The calm, clear centre of a cyclone is called the
why: The eye has light winds and clear sky.

question: A rooftop water tank is placed high so that
b: Water reaches taps with enough pressure
why: Greater height of water gives greater pressure at taps below.

question: During a thunderstorm, which place is safest?
c: Inside a closed building or car
d: On a hilltop holding a metal rod
why: Closed buildings and vehicles protect from lightning; tall objects attract it.

question: A 60 kg boy has two feet each 150 cm squared on the floor. Taking g = 10 N/kg, his pressure on the floor is
why: Force 600 N; area 300 cm squared = 0.03 m squared; 600/0.03 = 20,000 Pa.

question: Water is poured to the same height in three vessels with bases of different areas. The pressure at the bottom of each is
why: Liquid pressure depends on height (depth), not on base area.

question: On a hot afternoon at the seashore, the land warms more than the sea. The wind blows

question: A hole is made at different heights in a tall bottle. Water squirts farthest from
why: Pressure is greatest at the lowest point, so water leaves with the greatest speed.

question: Why does the wind speed rise near the centre of a cyclone (eye wall)?

question: Two teams build windproof hoardings. Team X uses a solid sheet and Team Y uses sheets with many holes. Which is more likely to survive a strong storm and why?

question: Matter is made up of
why: All matter is made of tiny particles.

question: Ice turning into water is called

question: Which state of matter has no fixed shape and no fixed volume?

question: A drop of ink spreads fastest in
why: Particles move faster at higher temperature.

question: During boiling of water at 100 degrees C, the particles
b: Gain enough energy to separate and become vapour
why: Heat energy overcomes the attraction between the particles.

question: Why does perfume spread faster in a room than a drop of honey spreads in a cup of water?

question: A syringe filled with air can be compressed but one filled with water cannot be compressed easily. Why?

question: A drop of dye is placed in a glass of water without stirring. After some time the colour is uniform. This shows
a: Particles of liquid are in constant motion

why: Random motion of particles leads to mixing.

question: Which statement explains why a solid keeps its shape but a liquid does not?

question: A student heats naphthalene balls in a covered dish and sees white crystals on the cold lid. Which describes what happened?
